plan.title: Synthetic MSE cognitive challenges
plan.target: mean-squared estimation error and bias-variance reasoning

questions.prompt: X equals 0 or 2 with equal probability. Compute E[X].
questions.feedback_wrong: Use the given probabilities to form a weighted average.

questions.prompt: State the mean-squared error definition for an estimator T of a fixed target theta. Identify the random and fixed quantities and a moment assumption.
questions.solution: MSE(T;theta)=E[(T-theta)^2]. T is random under the sampling model; theta is the fixed target. A finite second moment ensures finite MSE.
criteria: Express an expected squared estimation error.
Identify T as random and theta as fixed.
State finite second moment for the expectation to be finite.

questions.prompt: The estimation error is -2 or +2 with equal probability. Explain why mean error zero can coexist with a nonzero MSE. Use this example to distinguish cancellation from squared loss.
questions.solution: The mean error is (-2+2)/2=0. Each squared error is 4, so MSE is 4. Signed cancellation does not make the estimator exact.
criteria: Explain that opposite signed errors cancel in their mean.
Explain that squaring produces two positive losses and compute their mean.

questions.prompt: An estimator T takes 0 or 2, each with probability one half, while the fixed target theta is 2. Compute its dimensionless MSE.
questions.solution: The errors are -2 and 0; their squared losses are 4 and 0. MSE=(4+0)/2=2.
questions.feedback_wrong: Compute the error relative to theta in each support case, square it and average with the given probabilities.

questions.prompt: A derivation claims E[(T-theta)^2]=E[T^2]-theta^2 for every estimator T and fixed theta. Locate the missing term, state exactly when the claim holds, and give one counterexample.
questions.solution: The expansion is E[T^2]-2 theta E[T]+theta^2. The proposed formula is equal only when theta(E[T]-theta)=0. For constant T=0 and theta=1, actual MSE is 1 but the proposed expression is -1.
criteria: Expand the square and identify the omitted mean term.
State equality holds if theta is zero or E[T]=theta.
Provide and verify a finite-second-moment counterexample.

questions.prompt: Under one fixed sampling model, estimator A is unbiased with variance 4; estimator B has bias 1 and variance 2. Evaluate the claim that unbiasedness alone always makes A preferable for squared-error loss. State the scope and limitations of your conclusion.
questions.solution: For squared-error loss and finite second moments, MSE(A)=4 and MSE(B)=2+1=3. B has smaller MSE here, despite its bias. This ordering need not hold under another sampling model, target or loss.
criteria: Use variance plus squared bias to compare the two stated risks.
Reject unbiasedness alone as a sufficient ordering for MSE.
Limit the conclusion to this model, target and squared-error loss; do not claim universal estimator superiority.

questions.prompt: Design a synthetic two-point estimator for a fixed target theta=0 with bias 1 and MSE 3. Give its support and normalized probabilities, verify the moments, and explain why this design does not establish the best estimator in a real experiment.
questions.solution: One valid design is T=0 with probability 2/3 and T=3 with probability 1/3. The mean is 1 and second moment is 3, giving bias 1 and MSE 3 at theta=0. Many constructions are valid; without a real sampling model and decision constraints this is only a synthetic example.
criteria: Specify two support values and nonnegative probabilities summing to one.
Verify mean 1, hence bias 1, and second moment/MSE 3.
Discuss valid alternatives and the missing real sampling-model and decision constraints.

segments.title: Mean squared error
covers: mean squared error and its assumptions

steps.say: Mean squared error averages the squared difference between a random estimator and its fixed target. Finite second moments make this risk finite.
